hero.name: Kamala
hero.who: a retired schoolteacher in Madurai, adrift since her husband died last winter

story.b: Every morning at six, Kamala still makes two cups of filter coffee before she remembers. Her husband Raghavan died last winter, after forty-one years of marriage. Her son calls from Pune every Sunday and asks if she is eating. She says yes. She is, mostly. But the days have gone flat. She waters the tulsi, watches the noon news, naps, and waits for the evening to end. For thirty years she taught maths at the corporation school, and now nobody needs her at nine o'clock. Her neighbour Lakshmi invites her to the temple and to a wedding. Kamala goes once, smiles politely, and comes home early. At night she wonders, quietly and without drama, what all of this is for now.

ask.q: Kamala feels her days have no point since her husband died. What would help her most right now?
o: Keep busy every hour with errands so there is no time to think
Wait alone, since grief will lift by itself if she gives it time
Talk to someone she trusts, and slowly look for a reason her days still matter
ask.why: Grief needs company, not only time. Talking to someone she trusts eases the weight, and looking for a reason to get up gives her days a direction. Errands fill the hours without filling the emptiness, and waiting alone can stretch a heavy season into a lonely one.

chapters.take: When the days feel empty, the deepest need is a reason, not a distraction.

story.b: One evening Lakshmi's granddaughter Divya knocks with a maths notebook full of red marks. Her Class 10 boards are in March, and algebra makes her cry. Kamala says she can come for one hour after school. The next morning Kamala wakes before the alarm. She finds her old chalk box, sorts problems from easy to hard, and buys a packet of Marie biscuits for the sessions. In the second week the power goes off for six hours and the flat is like an oven. Another day her knees ache badly. Both times she still sits with Divya by the window, fanning herself with a newspaper. The heat is the same as last month. But now it no longer crushes her.

ask.q: The sessions have lifted Kamala's days, but her son suggests she stop, since teaching tires her knees. What should Kamala do?
o: Keep the sessions, perhaps shorter, because a reason to get up matters more than comfort
Stop the sessions completely so she can rest and avoid any strain
Take on ten students at once to fill every empty hour
ask.why: The sessions give Kamala something rest alone cannot: a reason her effort matters to someone. Shorter sessions protect her knees and keep the purpose. Stopping brings back the hollow days, and ten students turns a meaningful hour into a draining routine just to stay busy.

chapters.take: A clear reason to show up makes hard days bearable.

story.b: The family pension still has not started. Kamala goes to the bank on Town Hall Road for the third time, carrying a plastic folder of certificates. The queue is long, the fan is broken, and the clerk sighs when he sees her file. A missing signature, he says, come back next week. On the bus home she feels the old anger rise, at the bank, at the paperwork, at being alone with all of it. Then she notices she still has a choice. She cannot make the bank faster. She can decide how she carries this. That night she writes a neat list of every document, calls a family friend who works in a bank, and sleeps without replaying the clerk's face.

ask.q: The clerk sends Kamala away again over a small missing signature. What is the wisest way for her to respond?
o: Argue loudly at the counter until someone senior gives in
Decide to stay calm and firm, then plan her next step clearly
Give up on the pension, since the system is clearly against her
ask.why: The delay is out of her hands, but her response is not. Staying calm and firm keeps her dignity and lets her act clearly. Shouting may feel good for a moment yet often slows things down, and giving up hands her freedom to a broken counter.

chapters.take: You may not choose what happens, but you choose how you meet it.

story.b: Kamala's week slowly takes a shape. Mornings are for preparing Divya's lessons. On Wednesday evenings she video calls her grandson Adithya in Pune and teaches him one Tamil rhyme, clapping the beat while he giggles. On Sundays she cooks rasam with Lakshmi, and they share it on the terrace. Some days the grief still arrives without warning, at the sound of a scooter like Raghavan's. On those days she lets herself cry, then waters the jasmine plant he loved. One Sunday, over the rasam, Lakshmi sighs. She says Kamala is lucky to have found a purpose, because she herself has none, just grandchildren and a garden. Kamala looks at her friend, surprised.

ask.q: Lakshmi says she has no purpose, only grandchildren and a garden. What could Kamala gently tell her?
o: That she should find one big mission, like starting a charity
That purpose is only for younger people with careers ahead
That caring for her grandchildren and her garden are real sources of meaning
ask.why: Meaning rarely needs a grand mission. It often lives in the work we do, the people we love and how we carry hard things. Lakshmi already has two of these. Pushing her toward a big cause misses what she has, and calling purpose a young person's thing is simply untrue.

chapters.take: Meaning often hides in ordinary work, love and the way we carry pain.

story.h: The boy on the ground floor
story.b: Prakash from the ground floor is twenty-six and looks much older these days. His mother had a stroke in June, and now he does everything, from tablets at eight to changing sheets at midnight. One evening Kamala finds him sitting on the steps with his head in his hands. She knows that look. She spent Raghavan's last year in and out of the district hospital, counting drips and sleeping on plastic chairs. For months afterwards, that year felt like pure loss. Sitting beside Prakash, she realises it has given her something. She knows which forms the hospital needs, which nurse to ask, and how lonely the night hours feel. She makes him a cup of coffee and stays.

ask.q: Prakash says caring for his mother feels pointless and crushing. What is the kindest, most useful thing Kamala can offer?
o: Tell him to stay positive, because others have it much worse
Listen, share how seeing care as love helped her, and help him find support and rest
Advise him to hide his tiredness so his mother does not feel guilty
ask.why: Kamala's own hard year now has a use: she can recognise his pain and share what helped. Seeing care as an act of love can lighten the weight, and support and rest keep him going. Comparing his pain to others dismisses it, and hiding exhaustion only makes it heavier.

chapters.take: Pain you cannot avoid feels lighter when it serves something you love.

story.b: Her son, worried, sends Kamala an app that asks her to rate her happiness every night from one to ten. For a week she obeys. She buys a new silk saree, visits a mall in a cousin's car, and still taps a five each night. Checking so often makes her feel worse, as if she is failing a test. Then comes the Saturday Divya gets her half-yearly result: sixty-eight in maths, up from thirty-one. The girl runs up three floors waving the paper. Kamala spends the whole afternoon helping her plan the next chapters and forgets the app entirely. Only at night does she notice she has been smiling for hours.

ask.q: Kamala's son wants her to keep rating her happiness every night to track her recovery. What should she do?
o: Drop the daily score, and keep giving her time to the people and work she cares about
Keep rating it, and buy herself a small treat whenever the number drops
Rate it morning and night as well, so she can catch low moods early
ask.why: Happiness tends to arrive as a side effect of caring about something beyond yourself. Constant scoring turns it into an exam she keeps failing. Treats give a short lift and fade, and checking more often only feeds the worry. Absorbed in Divya's progress, she felt good without trying.

chapters.take: Chase happiness and it slips away. Give yourself to something worthwhile and it follows.

story.b: By February, Kamala makes one cup of coffee in the morning, and it no longer feels like a loss. Her living room has become a small evening classroom. Divya brings two friends now, and the plastic folder of pension papers has been replaced by a box of chalk. The pension finally started in December. Prakash's mother is home and stable, and he comes up on Sundays to share rasam with Kamala and Lakshmi. Some evenings are still heavy. She still misses Raghavan's voice calling her from the balcony. But when someone asks how she is, she does not reach for a number. She talks about Divya's exam date, and what she will teach next week.

chapters.take: A life with a reason in it can hold both grief and joy.
